clinicalPearls: Decompression sickness arises when ambient pressure falls too quickly, as after diving ascents, tunnel and caisson work, or aircraft or altitude-chamber exposure, allowing dissolved inert gas to form bubbles
Type I (mild) disease features joint and limb pain ('the bends'), skin mottling and itching, and lymphatic swelling
Type II (serious) disease involves the nervous system, lungs or inner ear, with limb weakness, numbness, bladder dysfunction, breathlessness ('the chokes') or vertigo, and is a medical emergency
Symptoms usually appear within minutes to hours of surfacing or pressure reduction, and delayed onset can occur particularly after flying soon after diving
First aid centres on high-flow oxygen, keeping the patient flat and hydrated, and urgent contact with a diving or hyperbaric medicine service
Definitive treatment is recompression in a hyperbaric chamber followed by a staged decompression, and this should not be delayed
Arterial gas embolism from pulmonary barotrauma can present similarly with sudden collapse or stroke-like signs and is managed along the same emergency pathway
Prevention relies on adherence to decompression schedules, controlled ascent rates and avoiding flying too soon after diving
reference.pathophysiology: During exposure to raised pressure, inert gas (usually nitrogen) dissolves into body tissues in proportion to the pressure and time. If pressure is reduced faster than the gas can be safely eliminated through the lungs, it comes out of solution and forms bubbles within tissues and blood. These bubbles cause mechanical obstruction of vessels, mechanical tissue distortion, and secondary inflammatory and coagulation responses, producing the musculoskeletal, neurological, pulmonary and other manifestations.
additionalDifferentials: Arterial gas embolism from pulmonary barotrauma
Stroke or other acute neurological event
Cardiac or respiratory causes of collapse
additionalInvestigations: Detailed dive or pressure exposure profile including depth, times and ascent rate
Neurological examination to detect spinal cord and cerebral involvement
Early consultation with a hyperbaric medicine specialist
Imaging where an alternative diagnosis such as stroke is being considered, without delaying recompression
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: any neurological features, breathlessness or collapse after decompression require immediate high-flow oxygen and urgent recompression
Rapid deterioration or evolving spinal cord signs such as leg weakness or urinary retention
Sudden collapse or stroke-like presentation suggesting arterial gas embolism
reference.prognosis: Prompt recompression and oxygen therapy give a good chance of full recovery, especially in milder disease; delay in treatment, severe neurological involvement or arterial gas embolism carry a higher risk of permanent deficit.
pitfalls: Dismissing joint pain or vague symptoms after diving as musculoskeletal and missing early DCS
Delaying recompression while arranging non-essential investigations
Failing to give continuous high-flow oxygen during transfer
Overlooking the risk of flying or altitude exposure soon after diving
Assuming that a symptom-free interval excludes serious disease
management: Give high-flow oxygen and keep the patient lying flat and well hydrated as first aid
Arrange urgent recompression in a hyperbaric chamber followed by staged decompression as the definitive treatment, without delay
Consult a hyperbaric or diving medicine specialist early
Treat serious type II neurological, pulmonary or inner-ear disease as a medical emergency
Avoid any further pressure reduction, including flying, until cleared by a diving physician
In occupational settings, review the pressure exposure profile and reinforce safe decompression schedules to prevent recurrence
